children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start by beginning an eligibility assessment.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Let me start by asking you about the children you're applying for.

**How old is the child (or children) that you're claiming Child Benefit for?**

Please tell me:
- The child's name and age (or date of birth)
- If you have more than one child, please list all of them

This will help me determine which eligibility rules apply to your situation.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm asking about my son Alex - he's 6 years old.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! Alex is 6 years old, which means he falls into the **under 16 category** - excellent news, as children under 16 generally have a straightforward path to qualifying for Child Benefit.

Now let me check the next eligibility requirement. Since Alex is under 16, I need to verify one important thing:

**Is Alex working full-time in paid employment?**

This is just to confirm he's not in full-time paid work, which would affect eligibility. For a 6-year-old, the answer is almost certainly no, but I need to ask to follow the proper assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not working at all - he's just in primary school.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! That's exactly what we'd expect for a 6-year-old. Since Alex is under 16 and not working full-time, he qualifies as a "qualifying child" for Child Benefit purposes.

Now I need to check some additional eligibility requirements that apply to you as the person claiming. Let me navigate through the next steps.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Great! Since Alex is not working, let me move forward to the next check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Is Alex receiving any benefits in his own right, such as Employment and Support Allowance or Universal Credit?**

For a 6-year-old in primary school, the answer would typically be no, but I need to confirm this.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he doesn't get any benefits himself.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Let me continue with the next check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Is Alex in any type of apprenticeship?**

This is another question where, for a 6-year-old in primary school, the answer would be no. But let me confirm.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not in an apprenticeship - he's only 6!

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Of course! That's a fair point. Let me proceed to the next important check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check your residency status. This is an important requirement for Child Benefit eligibility.

**Where do you normally live, and what is your residency status?**

Here are the main scenarios:

1. **Do you normally live in the UK?** (This covers most people)

2. **Or do you have any of these statuses:**
   - Settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme
   - Pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme (with additional requirements like working, studying, or having sufficient resources)
   - Are you a Crown servant living abroad in certain qualifying countries?

What best describes your situation?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I live in the UK - I'm in Manchester with Alex.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! You normally live in the UK, which satisfies the residency requirement. Let me move forward:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good! Now I need to confirm that you're responsible for Alex. This means either:

1. **You live with him** (which you've already told me - you're both in Manchester)
2. OR you contribute to his upkeep
3. OR you're paying maintenance under a court order

Since you live with Alex, this is clearly satisfied. Let me continue:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Important question: Is anyone else currently claiming Child Benefit for Alex, or is there any other person who also has responsibility for him and might be claiming?**

This could include:
- Alex's other parent
- Another family member
- Another carer

Or are you the only person claiming for him?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for him - it's just me.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Great! That's clear. Let me continue:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Where is Alex living? Is he:**

1. In hospital for treatment?
2. In local authority care?
3. Fostered with another family?
4. Living with you at home normally?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, he has been in local authority care, but he comes home to stay with me regularly.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying that. This is an important detail. Let me ask a bit more to understand the exact arrangement:

**Can you tell me more about Alex's care arrangement:**

1. Is he currently in local authority care full-time, but comes home to stay with you regularly (like weekends or holidays)?
2. Or has he been in local authority care in the past, but is now living with you at home permanently?
3. How often does he stay with you - is it regular overnight stays, or just daytime visits?

This will help me determine which specific rules apply to Alex's situation.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's currently in care but he comes home to stay with me every weekend - so he spends quite a bit of time at home with me.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Thank you for that detail. So Alex is currently in local authority care but spends weekends at home with you. Let me navigate to the relevant check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
This is a key question for Alex's situation. Let me clarify:

**Regarding Alex's time at home with you while he's in care:**

1. **How long has Alex been in local authority care?** (Is it 8 weeks or less, or longer than 8 weeks?)

2. **How many hours does Alex spend at home with you each week?** (You mentioned every weekend - is that at least 24 hours per week? For example, if he comes Friday evening through Sunday evening, that would typically be around 48 hours.)

If either of these is true, Alex can still qualify:
- He's been in care for 8 weeks or less, OR
- He spends at least 24 hours per week at home

What's the situation with these timeframes?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's been in care for a couple of months now. But yes, when he comes home on weekends it's definitely more than 24 hours - he's usually with me from Friday evening through Sunday afternoon.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! That's exactly what matters. Alex has been in care for a couple of months (which is more than 8 weeks), BUT he spends well over 24 hours per week at home with you (Friday evening through Sunday afternoon is roughly 48+ hours per week). This means he still qualifies for Child Benefit.

Let me continue:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! We're almost there. One final question:

**Is the local council paying towards Alex's accommodation or maintenance while he's in care?**

In most cases where a child is in local authority care, the council does pay for their accommodation and upkeep. However, I need to confirm this to complete the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, the local authority is paying for his care while he's there.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I appreciate you providing that information. Let me work through this carefully, as this is an important detail.

You've told me that:
- Alex is in local authority care
- The local authority is paying for his accommodation and maintenance while he's in care
- He spends weekends with you (Friday evening through Sunday afternoon - over 24 hours per week)

Based on the eligibility rules, when a local council is paying for a child's accommodation and maintenance, this typically means you cannot receive Child Benefit for that child, even if they spend time at home with you.

However, I want to make sure I have the complete picture. Let me ask:

**When Alex is at home with you on weekends, are you contributing anything towards his upkeep during those times?** For example:
- Do you provide his meals while he's with you?
- Do you buy him clothes or necessities?
- Do you provide pocket money or other financial support?

This could potentially affect the outcome, as responsibility and contribution to upkeep are relevant factors.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, of course I do! When he's home with me I feed him, buy his clothes, and give him pocket money. I'm still his parent even though he's in care during the week.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
That's completely understandable, and you're absolutely right - you're still his parent and you do contribute to his upkeep when he's with you. However, I need to follow the specific eligibility rules as set out in the Child Benefit regulations.

Let me check the exact requirements by getting the validation rules to ensure I'm interpreting this correctly:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for getting that clarification. I can see from the validation rules that there's an important rule about council payments. Let me navigate to the final eligibility determination:

Based on the rules, when a local council is paying for a child's accommodation or maintenance, you generally cannot claim Child Benefit for that child. This rule exists even when:
- You're still the child's parent
- You contribute to their upkeep when they're at home
- They spend significant time with you

The rule is quite clear: "Generally cannot claim if local council is paying for child's accommodation or maintenance."

However, I want to be thorough and check if there are any exceptions I should consider. Let me navigate to see the outcome:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I'm sorry to inform you that based on the eligibility rules, **you are not eligible for Child Benefit for Alex** at this time.

**The reason:** The local authority is paying towards Alex's accommodation and maintenance while he is in their care. The Child Benefit rules state that you generally cannot claim if the local council is paying for the child's accommodation or maintenance.

**What this means:**
- Even though you're still his parent
- Even though you contribute to his upkeep when he's home at weekends
- Even though he spends significant time with you (over 24 hours per week)
- The fact that the council is paying for his accommodation and maintenance means you cannot currently claim

**What might change this:**
If Alex's care arrangement changes and he is no longer in local authority care (or if the council is no longer paying for his accommodation/maintenance), you would be able to claim Child Benefit again. At that point, you should contact the Child Benefit Office to restart your claim.

**Next steps:**
- You can contact the Child Benefit Office if your circumstances change
- If you have questions about this decision, you can appeal or ask for clarification from HMRC
- It may be worth discussing with the local authority about any potential changes to Alex's care arrangement

I understand this is disappointing news given your continued involvement in Alex's care. Is there anything else you'd like me to clarify about this decision?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Oh, I see. That's disappointing, but I understand. Thank you for explaining it all clearly to me.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
You're very welcome. I'm glad I could walk you through the process clearly, even though the outcome isn't what you hoped for.

**Remember:**
- This situation can change. If Alex's care arrangement changes or the council stops paying for his maintenance, you'd be able to claim again
- You can always contact the Child Benefit Office if your circumstances change, and they can help you restart a claim
- Your continued support and contributions during his weekends at home are still very important for Alex

If you have any other questions about Child Benefit eligibility in the future, or if your circumstances do change, feel free to reach out. I'm here to help.

Best of luck with everything, and I hope things work out well for you and Alex.

conversation.text: Thank you so much for your help and for being so thorough. I really appreciate you taking the time to explain everything. Take care!

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
You're very welcome! I'm so glad I could help you understand the situation thoroughly. You were a pleasure to work with, and I really appreciated how you provided clear answers to all the questions.

Take care of yourself and Alex. All the best to you both! 😊

If you ever need help with Child Benefit eligibility in the future, don't hesitate to reach out. Goodbye!

reasonings: Alex is 6 years old (under 16, meeting the age requirement). He is not working full-time, does not receive benefits in his own right, and is not in a disqualifying apprenticeship. This disqualifies the claim despite the claimant's continued parental involvement and financial contributions during Alex's time at home.
arguments.overall_reasoning: The claimant is not eligible for Child Benefit for Alex. While Alex meets all the standard eligibility criteria (age, residency, not working, no disqualifying factors) and the claimant meets responsibility requirements (living with the child and contributing to upkeep), the claim fails on the council payments criterion. age_and_education.rule: Child must be under 16, OR aged 16-19 and in approved education or training
age_and_education.approved_education: Full-time non-advanced education (12+ hours/week supervised study): A-levels, T-levels, Scottish Highers, NVQ Level 3 or below
age_and_education.advanced_education_excluded: University degrees, HNC (Level 4), HND (Level 5), NVQ Level 4+, professional qualifications Level 4+
age_and_education.minimum_hours: 12 hours per week supervised study required for 16-19 year olds
age_and_education.approved_training: Unpaid work-based training with education provider, or approved training course. Employer-funded training excluded.
age_and_education.extension: If 16-17 year old leaves education/training, benefit continues for 20 weeks if registered with careers service, Connexions, or armed services. Ends at week 20 or age 18, whichever sooner.
age_and_education.birthday_cutoff: Benefit stops on child's 20th birthday, not at end of academic year
age_and_education.married_children: Married 16-19 year olds only qualify if financially dependent on claimant
ending_conditions: Child starts paid work 24+ hours per week and leaves education/training
Child receives ESA, Universal Credit, or similar benefits in own right
Child starts advanced education (university, HNC, HND)

apprenticeship_rules.england: ALL apprenticeships disqualify (Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, Degree)
apprenticeship_rules.wales: Foundation Apprenticeships APPROVED. Other Welsh apprenticeships disqualify.
apprenticeship_rules.note: Welsh Foundation Apprenticeships are the ONLY apprenticeships that qualify for Child Benefit

residency.rule: Must normally live in UK or meet special circumstances
residency.settled_status: Can claim with settled status under EU Settlement Scheme
presettled_status_conditions: Working and earning above NI primary threshold for 3 continuous months, OR
Looking for work (jobseeker for up to 91 days), OR
Sufficient resources (not claiming IS, JSA, PC, UC), OR
Family member of EEA/Swiss national with right to reside
residency.abroad: May qualify if Crown servant or living in certain countries

responsibility.rule: Must be responsible for child through living with them OR contributing to upkeep
responsibility.contributing: Must pay at least Child Benefit amount (or equivalent in kind) towards care
responsibility.contribution_threshold: £26.05 per week for eldest/only child, £17.25 per week for additional children (2024/25 rates - check gov.uk for current rates)
responsibility.frequency: Can be weekly, monthly, or lump sum
responsibility.combined_contributions: Two people can combine contributions if both contribute to same child

unequal_allocation.rule: When contributing to multiple children, can allocate contribution amounts unequally
unequal_allocation.explanation: If contributing £40 for two children, can allocate as £26.05 (eldest) + £13.95 (second), or any split where each child receives at least their applicable rate
unequal_allocation.example_1: £40 total for 2 children: £26.05 (child 1) + £13.95 (child 2) = eligible for child 1 only
unequal_allocation.example_2: £50 total for 2 children: £26.05 (child 1) + £23.95 (child 2) = eligible for both
unequal_allocation.note: Each child must receive at least the Child Benefit rate they would generate (eldest rate for first child, additional rate for others)

responsibility.adoption_allowance: Adoption allowance does NOT disqualify (unlike fostering allowance)

priority_rules.rule: Only one person can claim Child Benefit for a child
priority_rules.multiple_carers: If two people are responsible, they must agree who claims

hmrc_arbitration.rule: If agreement cannot be reached, HMRC decides based on evidence
criteria: Primary residence (where child spends most nights per week)
Main contributor to child's upkeep and care
Day-to-day care responsibilities
Stability and continuity for the child
Existing claim history
evidence_required: Proof of residence (utility bills, rental agreement, council tax)
Financial contribution evidence (bank statements, receipts, maintenance records)
Court orders or formal custody arrangements (if applicable)
Statements from child's school, doctor, or other professionals
common_scenarios: Separated parents with child spending 4 days vs 3 days per week with each
Grandparent caring for grandchild while parent works
Child living part-time with two different households
Parent vs step-parent both contributing significantly
hmrc_arbitration.appeal_process: Contact Child Benefit Office if circumstances change significantly

priority_rules.transfer: Current claimant can transfer by contacting Child Benefit Office
priority_rules.child_moves: If child moves but you still contribute to upkeep (at least CB amount), you can continue claiming

hospital.time_limit: 12 weeks in hospital or residential accommodation
hospital.linking_rule: CUMULATIVE: If child returns within 28 days, time counts towards 12-week limit. Multiple stays within 28 days add together.
hospital.example: 10 weeks + 15 day gap + 3 weeks = 13 weeks cumulative (exceeds limit)
hospital.exception: Can continue if regularly spending money on child
hospital.abroad: For hospital abroad, only if went for treatment and you're back in UK spending on them
hospital.mental_health: Psychiatric units count as hospital, not custody

care.exception_24_hours: Can continue if child spends 24+ hours per week at home
care.exception_nights: Can continue if child spends 2 consecutive nights per week at home
care.reclaim_conditions: Can claim again if child spends 2 consecutive nights/week OR 7+ consecutive days at home
care.custody: Youth custody counts as care, 8-week limit applies

hospital_and_care.partner_spending: Partner's money only counts if married/civil partnered and living together

council_payments.rule: Generally cannot claim if local council is paying for child's accommodation or maintenance
council_payments.fostering: Can claim for fostered child only if council NOT paying
council_payments.informal_care: Cannot claim if council paying for informal care arrangement

administrative.backdating: Claims can be backdated up to 3 months

high_income_charge.rule: HICBC is a payment adjustment, not an eligibility criterion. Claimant is still eligible but may owe tax.
high_income_charge.calculation: Tax charge = 1% of Child Benefit for every £200 of income between £60k-£80k
high_income_charge.who_pays: Higher earner in household pays, regardless of who claims Child Benefit
examples: Income £80,000+: 100% clawback (but still eligible, just repay full amount)
high_income_charge.opt_out: Can choose not to receive payments to avoid charge, but should still register to protect National Insurance credits
high_income_charge.partner_income: Partner's income applies even if they are not the claimant. Higher earner always pays.
high_income_charge.not_eligibility: Important: HICBC does NOT affect eligibility. It is a post-payment tax charge only.

payment_structure.eldest_child_rate: Higher rate for first child claimed
payment_structure.additional_children_rate: Lower rate for each additional child
payment_structure.split_family_rule: If two parents each claim for different children from same family, both get eldest child rate for their first child
payment_structure.example: Divorced parents: Mother claims for child A (gets eldest rate), Father claims for child B (also gets eldest rate, not additional rate)
payment_structure.frequency: Paid every 4 weeks, or weekly if single parent or receiving certain benefits
